nodes.label: Britain
nodes.full: The former protecting power: the 1899 agreement and the 1961 guarantee that brought British troops back to deter Iraq, and the protection Kuwait then transferred to the United States.
nodes.src: background — the Anglo-Kuwaiti agreements.

nodes.label: Iraq
nodes.full: The northern neighbour: claimant to Kuwait in 1961, its funded ally in the 1980s war, and its invader and seven-month occupier in 1990–91.
nodes.src: background — the historiography of Iraqi–Kuwaiti relations.

nodes.label: The United States
nodes.full: The security guarantor after 1987: the reflagging of Kuwaiti tankers, the 1991 liberation, the bases, and the staging ground for the 2003 invasion of Iraq.
nodes.src: background — the US–Kuwait Defence Cooperation Agreement (1991).

nodes.label: Iran
nodes.full: The revolutionary republic across the Gulf: it attacked Kuwaiti shipping in the tanker war and remains the pole of a regional confrontation that strains Kuwait's Sunni–Shiʿi balance.
nodes.src: background — Louër, 'Transnational Shia Politics' (2008).

nodes.label: The oil market
nodes.full: The demand and price for crude: roughly 90 percent of Kuwait's revenue, the basis of the rentier bargain, and the constraint on the budget when prices fall.
nodes.src: background — the IMF Article IV consultations.

nodes.label: Sheikh ʿAbdullāh III al-Sālim
nodes.full: Led Kuwait to independence from Britain on 19 June 1961, promulgated the 1962 Constitution with its elected National Assembly — the most liberal in the Gulf — and faced down the first Iraqi claim on the country.
nodes.src: the Anglo-Kuwaiti exchange of notes (19 June 1961); the Constitution of Kuwait (11 November 1962).

nodes.label: Sheikh Ṣabāḥ III al-Sālim
nodes.full: The oil-boom years and the first dissolution of parliament in 1976, which the emir suspended for four years — the first breach of the constitutional order.
nodes.src: the 1976 emiri decree dissolving the National Assembly; Jill Crystal, 'Oil and Politics in the Gulf' (1990).

nodes.label: Sheikh Jābir al-Aḥmad
nodes.full: The long reign — the Souk al-Manakh crash of 1982, the Iran–Iraq tanker war, the 1985 assassination attempt, the Iraqi invasion and the emir's flight to Ṭāʾif, the liberation, and women's suffrage granted in his last year.
nodes.src: Michael Herb, 'The Wages of Oil' (2014); the events of 1990–91 in Kuwait's official record.

nodes.label: Sheikh Ṣabāḥ IV al-Aḥmad
nodes.full: Reached the throne in the January 2006 succession crisis, when the ailing Saʿd al-ʿAbdullāh abdicated as the Assembly moved to depose him. Fourteen years as emir and as the Gulf's leading diplomatic mediator.
nodes.src: the National Assembly's role in the 2006 succession; the UN's naming of him 'Humanitarian Leader' (2014).

nodes.label: Sheikhs Nawāf and Mishʿal
nodes.full: Nawāf al-Aḥmad (2020–2023), then his half-brother Mishʿal al-Aḥmad, who in May 2024 dissolved the National Assembly and suspended parts of the constitution for up to four years — a pause in Kuwait's parliamentary experiment.
nodes.src: the emiri address of 10 May 2024 suspending the Assembly; this entry records the position as of early 2026.

nodes.label: The crown prince as prime minister
nodes.full: For forty years the heir apparent also headed the government, fusing the succession and the executive and keeping both firmly inside the ruling family.
nodes.src: Herb, 'All in the Family' (1999); the 2003 separation of the two offices.

nodes.label: The separation of the offices and the cabinet crises
nodes.full: From 2003 the premiership went to other senior sheikhs, and the following two decades saw a rapid churn of cabinets — dozens of them — each brought down by clashes with the elected Assembly over corruption, spending and ministerial questioning.
nodes.src: the government-formation record 2003–2024; the recurring 'grillings' (istijwāb) of ministers.

nodes.label: The Iraqi claim and the 1961 crisis
nodes.full: Days after independence, ʿAbd al-Karīm Qāsim's Iraq claimed Kuwait as part of Basra province; British and then Arab League troops deployed, and Iraq formally recognised Kuwait in 1963 — a claim that was never fully renounced.
nodes.src: the UN Security Council debates of 1961; the 1963 Iraqi–Kuwaiti agreed minutes.

nodes.label: The Iran–Iraq War spillover
nodes.full: Kuwait bankrolled Iraq's war effort and saw its tankers attacked by Iran in reprisal; in 1987 it obtained the reflagging and naval escort of its ships by both the United States and the Soviet Union, drawing the superpowers into the Gulf.
nodes.src: the 'Earnest Will' reflagging operation (1987); Michael Palmer, 'On Course to Desert Storm' (1992).

nodes.label: The Iraqi invasion and occupation
nodes.full: Iraq overran Kuwait in a day, annexed it as its nineteenth province, looted and terrorised it for seven months, held foreign 'human shields', and on its retreat set some 700 oil wells alight.
nodes.src: UN Security Council Resolution 660 (2 August 1990); the reports of the occupation by Amnesty International and the Kuwaiti government (flagged: the parties' accounts differ on scale).

nodes.label: The liberation and the oil fires
nodes.full: The Coalition's Operation Desert Storm expelled the Iraqi army — the retreat up the 'Highway of Death' — and left behind months of burning wells, black skies and lakes of spilled oil, one of the worst deliberate environmental disasters on record.
nodes.src: UN Security Council Resolution 678 (1990); the environmental assessments of the oil fires (UNEP, the US Geological Survey).

nodes.label: Terrorism and the Shiʿi question
nodes.full: The 1983 bombings of Western and Kuwaiti targets, the 1985 attempt on Emir Jābir's life, and the 2015 Islamic State suicide bombing of the Imam Ṣādiq Shiʿi mosque that killed 27 — the external violence that has repeatedly tested Kuwait's Sunni–Shiʿi balance.
nodes.src: the 1983 Kuwait bombings; the June 2015 Imam Ṣādiq mosque attack, claimed by the Islamic State.

nodes.label: The 1962 Constitution
nodes.full: The most liberal constitution in the Gulf — an elected National Assembly with real legislative and oversight powers, a bill of rights, an independent judiciary — and an emir who nonetheless keeps the last word and the power to dissolve the Assembly.
nodes.src: the Constitution of the State of Kuwait (11 November 1962); Nathan Brown on the Kuwaiti constitutional order.

nodes.label: The suspension and revival of parliament
nodes.full: The Assembly has been dissolved or suspended again and again — the four-year suspensions of 1976 and 1986, and constitutionally many times since — each restored under public pressure, until the 2024 suspension for up to four years.
nodes.src: the dissolution decrees of 1976, 1986 and after; the pro-democracy movement of 1989–90; the emiri decision of 2024.

nodes.label: Oil nationalisation and the Future Generations Fund
nodes.full: The takeover of the Kuwait Oil Company (completed 1975), the creation of the Kuwait Petroleum Corporation (1980), and the Future Generations Fund — into which 10 percent of state revenue is placed each year for the day the oil runs out.
nodes.src: the 1976 law establishing the Future Generations Fund; the Kuwait Investment Authority, founded as the Kuwait Investment Board in 1953.

nodes.label: Women's suffrage
nodes.full: After decades of campaigning and repeated Assembly votes, women won the vote and the right to stand for election in May 2005; the first four women members were elected to the National Assembly in 2009.
nodes.src: the 2005 amendment to the electoral law; the 2009 election results.

nodes.label: The rentier social contract
nodes.full: No income tax, guaranteed public-sector employment for citizens, free health and education, subsidised fuel, water and power, and a housing grant — the bargain oil pays for, and the one Kuwait's frozen politics has made almost impossible to change.
nodes.src: the IMF Article IV consultations on Kuwait; Herb, 'The Wages of Oil' (2014).

nodes.label: The Islamists in the Assembly
nodes.full: The Muslim Brotherhood's Islamic Constitutional Movement and the Salafi blocs have been among the strongest and most consistent forces in the elected Assembly, driving legislation on morals, education and the courts across four decades.
nodes.src: Falah Abdullah al-Mdaires, 'Islamic Extremism in Kuwait'; the Islamist bloc results in successive elections.

nodes.label: The Shiʿi minority
nodes.full: Roughly a quarter to a third of the citizen body, historically loyal to the Āl Ṣabāḥ and with their own members of parliament, endowments and mosques — but under strain from the regional Sunni–Shiʿi confrontation and the 2015 mosque bombing.
nodes.src: Laurence Louër, 'Transnational Shia Politics' (2008); the Kuwaiti Shiʿi political blocs.

nodes.label: Faith among the non-citizen majority
nodes.full: Kuwait has several churches for its large Christian expatriate population, and a long-running public argument over whether the Hindu and other communities may build their own places of worship — the religious life of the 70 percent of residents who are not citizens.
nodes.src: the US State Department International Religious Freedom reports on Kuwait; the debate over non-Abrahamic worship.

nodes.label: The Kuwait Towers and the modern city
nodes.full: The 1979 water towers on the bay, the National Assembly building by Jørn Utzon (1982), the Al Hamra Tower and the Sheikh Jaber Al-Ahmad Cultural Centre (2016) — a modernist and then a monumental architecture built on oil.
nodes.src: the Kuwait Towers (Sune Lindström and Malene Björn); Utzon's National Assembly; the Kuwait National Cultural District.

nodes.label: The Kuwaiti novel
nodes.full: Ismāʿīl Fahd Ismāʿīl, the founder of the Kuwaiti novel, and Saud Alsanousi, whose 'The Bamboo Stalk' (2012) — about a half-Filipino Kuwaiti searching for a place in his father's country — won the International Prize for Arabic Fiction.
nodes.src: Saud Alsanousi, 'Sāq al-Bāmbū' (2012), IPAF winner 2013; the works of Ismāʿīl Fahd Ismāʿīl.

nodes.label: Kuwaiti television drama
nodes.full: From the 1960s Kuwait was the Gulf's leading producer of television serials, and the Ramadan drama remains a major cultural export and a vehicle for social commentary — on the family, the tribe, corruption and the expatriate presence.
nodes.src: the histories of Kuwaiti and Gulf television drama; the Ramadan-serial industry.

nodes.label: Sadu weaving and the museums
nodes.full: The Bedouin geometric weaving of the Sadu, on the UNESCO intangible-heritage list, kept alive by the Al Sadu Society, and the reconstructed National Museum and the Tareq Rajab collections — the deliberate curation of a pre-oil Kuwait.
nodes.src: the UNESCO inscription of 'al-Sadu, traditional weaving skills' (2020); the Kuwait National Museum, damaged in 1990 and rebuilt.

nodes.label: The diwaniyya as a political institution
nodes.full: The male evening salon, held in a room off the house, is where Kuwaiti politics is conducted — candidates campaign there, movements are organised there, and the 1989–90 movement that forced the restoration of parliament was run out of the diwaniyyas.
nodes.src: Mary Ann Tétreault, 'Stories of Democracy: Politics and Society in Contemporary Kuwait' (2000).

nodes.label: The Kuwaiti press
nodes.full: Once the freest press in the Arab world — home to al-Qabas, al-Rai and al-Anba, and a training ground for pan-Arab journalism — now more constrained by press and cybercrime laws, but still relatively open by regional standards.
nodes.src: the press-freedom assessments (Reporters Without Borders, Freedom House) tracking Kuwait's decline from the 2000s.

nodes.label: Documenting the occupation
nodes.full: The Kuwaiti and international record of the 1990–91 invasion — the war-crimes files, the missing-persons commission, the environmental studies of the oil fires, the museum of the occupation — a nation's forensic reckoning with seven months.
nodes.src: the Kuwaiti National Committee for Missing Persons and POW Affairs; the Al-Qurain Martyrs' Museum.

nodes.label: Oil, Burgan and the rentier state
nodes.full: The Greater Burgan field, one of the largest ever discovered, and an economy that draws roughly 90 percent of its revenue from oil and has never seriously diversified despite decades of plans.
nodes.src: the Kuwait Petroleum Corporation data; the IMF Article IV consultations on the oil dependence.

nodes.label: The Souk al-Manakh crash
nodes.full: An unofficial stock market operating out of a Kuwait City car park collapsed with an estimated 90 billion dollars of post-dated cheques outstanding — one of the largest financial crashes in history, which the state spent years absorbing.
nodes.src: the contemporary reporting; the Kuwaiti government's rescue and clearing programme.

nodes.label: The Kuwait Investment Authority
nodes.full: The world's oldest sovereign wealth fund, holding assets estimated in the several hundred billions, run at arm's length from the government — the country's insurance against the end of oil, and the buffer that funded the 1991 reconstruction.
nodes.src: the Kuwait Investment Authority; the sovereign-wealth-fund league tables.

nodes.label: The expatriate majority
nodes.full: Non-citizens are around 70 percent of the population — some three million of about 4.5 million — the workers who run the economy, under a kafala sponsorship system, and the 'demographic imbalance' is a permanent theme of Kuwaiti politics.
nodes.src: the Kuwait Public Authority for Civil Information population data; the recurring 'demographic imbalance' policy debates.

nodes.label: The reconstruction after 1990
nodes.full: The looted and burned country was rebuilt with sovereign-fund money and the oil revenue that resumed once the fires were out — one of the fastest post-war recoveries anywhere, though the political and psychological trauma outlasted the physical damage.
nodes.src: the World Bank and Kuwaiti government reconstruction assessments; the UN Compensation Commission awards.

nodes.label: Capping the oil fires
nodes.full: The international firefighting effort — the American teams of Red Adair and Boots & Coots, the Hungarian jet-engine 'Big Wind', and Kuwaiti, Iranian and Canadian crews — capped some 700 burning wells in eight months instead of the two to five years first predicted.
nodes.src: the accounts of the well-control campaign (Sahib Baroni; the Kuwait Oil Company).

nodes.label: Water from the sea
nodes.full: Kuwait meets essentially all of its water needs by desalination, one of the highest per-capita rates in the world, and the plants are strategic infrastructure — Iraqi forces damaged them during the 1990 occupation.
nodes.src: the Kuwait Ministry of Electricity and Water; the desalination-capacity figures.

nodes.label: Building against the heat
nodes.full: Kuwait is among the hottest inhabited places on earth — 53.9°C recorded at Mitribah in 2016 — and the total dependence on air-conditioning, the shaded design and the summer outdoor-work bans are the built and legal response to a worsening heat regime.
nodes.src: the WMO verification of the Mitribah record (2021); the studies of extreme heat and migrant outdoor labour in Kuwait.

nodes.label: Kuwait and the United States
nodes.full: A major non-NATO ally: the base for the 1991 liberation and the 2003 invasion of Iraq, host to large US installations at Camp Arifjan and Ali Al Salem, and the security guarantee that replaced the British protection ended in 1961.
nodes.src: the 1991 Defence Cooperation Agreement; the US designation of Kuwait as a major non-NATO ally (2004).

nodes.label: Kuwait and Iraq
nodes.full: The 1961 claim, the 1990 invasion, the UN border demarcation of 1993, the reparations that Iraq finished paying only in 2022, and the still-unresolved disputes over the Khawr ʿAbd Allāh waterway and the Mubārak al-Kabīr port.
nodes.src: UN Security Council Resolution 833 (1993) on the border; the UN Compensation Commission's final payment (February 2022).

nodes.label: Kuwait and Iran
nodes.full: A careful balance — trade and a shared Gulf, against the pull of the regional Sunni–Shiʿi confrontation, the spillover of the Iran–Iraq War, and Kuwait's own large Shiʿi minority.
nodes.src: Louër, 'Transnational Shia Politics' (2008); the Kuwaiti–Iranian relationship through the tanker war and after.

nodes.label: The mediator state
nodes.full: Kuwait's role, under Emir Ṣabāḥ IV especially, as the Gulf's diplomatic broker — the 2017–21 Qatar crisis, Yemen, intra-GCC disputes — a small state making neutrality and personal relationships an instrument of security.
nodes.src: the reporting on Kuwait's mediation of the 2017 Gulf crisis, ending with the Al-Ula declaration (2021).

nodes.label: Kuwaiti aid and the pan-Arab role
nodes.full: The Kuwait Fund for Arab Economic Development (1961), one of the oldest development funds anywhere in the global South, and Kuwait's long role as a financier of Arab and Palestinian causes — soft power bought with oil.
nodes.src: the Kuwait Fund for Arab Economic Development annual reports; the pre-1990 Palestinian community in Kuwait.

nodes.label: The Gulf's constitutional experiment
nodes.full: Kuwait built, and for six decades defended, the only elected parliament with real powers on the Arabian Peninsula — an experiment repeatedly suspended by the emir, repeatedly revived by public pressure, and, since 2024, paused.
nodes.src: Tétreault, 'Stories of Democracy' (2000); the 2024 suspension.

nodes.label: The war that redefined the Gulf
nodes.full: The invasion of Kuwait brought half a million American troops permanently into the region, split the Arab world between those who joined the Coalition and those who did not, and set the terms — the sanctions, the no-fly zones, the 2003 war — of everything that followed.
nodes.src: the historiography of the 1990–91 Gulf War as a regional turning point.

nodes.label: The unreformed rentier state
nodes.full: Kuwait has the sovereign fund, the constitution and the educated population to have diversified, and has not. As of the mid-2020s it runs budget deficits when oil is cheap, its megaprojects are stalled and its politics are frozen — a case study in a rich state that cannot change.
nodes.src: the IMF Article IV consultations (2020s); Herb, 'The Wages of Oil' (2014). This entry records the situation as of early 2026 and makes no prediction.

nodes.label: Women in the resistance and the vote
nodes.full: Kuwaiti women's prominent role in the 1990–91 occupation resistance — running networks, moving weapons and money, being detained, tortured and in some cases killed — is widely credited with breaking the argument against their enfranchisement, granted in 2005.
nodes.src: the accounts of the Kuwaiti women's resistance; the suffrage debate's use of the war record.

nodes.label: The Bidoon
nodes.full: Some 100,000 stateless residents, descended from those who did not register as citizens in 1959–61 — denied documents, formal work, schooling and healthcare, their situation a permanent grievance that successive governments have promised and failed to resolve.
nodes.src: Human Rights Watch, 'Prisoners of the Past: Kuwaiti Bidun' (2011) and later reports (advocacy source, flagged); the 2011 Bidoon protests.

nodes.label: The migrant workforce and kafala
nodes.full: The domestic workers, labourers and professionals who are 70 percent of the population, tied to a sponsor and — for domestic workers especially — exposed to non-payment and abuse; a 2015 domestic-worker law and later reforms have improved the legal position more than the reality.
nodes.src: the 2015 Domestic Labour Law; the ILO and Migrant-Rights.org reporting on Kuwait.

nodes.label: The town, the tribes and the ballot
nodes.full: The older merchant families of the town and the settled tribes of the desert edge form Kuwait's two social poles, and the electoral politics — the tribal primaries, the accusations of vote-buying, the redistricting — runs along that seam.
nodes.src: Michael Herb on the Kuwaiti electoral system; the periodic prosecutions over tribal primaries.
